text:
The investment case for sustainable offices in Africa is becoming easier to measure — and harder to dismiss as a purely environmental issue.

Our research looks at the growing divide between prime, efficient buildings and ageing secondary stock.

The strongest longitudinal evidence comes from South Africa. Green-certified Prime- and A-grade offices outperformed comparable non-certified buildings by a cumulative 28.2% over ten years. In 2025 they recorded lower vacancy, higher income per square metre and a lower operating cost-to-income ratio.

At the same time, the average additional construction cost associated with green-certified South African projects completed in 2022–24 was 2.40%.

Those figures do not prove that certification itself causes higher returns. Certified buildings are often newer, better located and better managed. That caveat matters.

But it may also point to the more important investment conclusion: sustainability is becoming part of what tenants, lenders and investors mean by a high-quality building.

Energy efficiency reduces exposure to operating costs. Solar and backup systems protect continuity. Water efficiency reduces resource risk. Certification gives lenders and occupiers a common way to assess performance. Multinational tenants increasingly bring their own environmental and procurement requirements.

The risk, then, is not only paying slightly more to build or retrofit a better asset. It is holding an apparently cheaper building whose income, occupancy and financing options weaken as the market moves around it.

That turns green building from an ESG add-on into an asset-resilience question.

For African property investors, where does the bigger risk now sit: the cost of upgrading buildings, or the cost of leaving older stock unchanged?
